sections.title: Two ways to hide who
sections.content: You know *se dice que* from B2 Unit 18 and impersonal *se* from B1 Unit 6. Spanish has two more ways to talk about people without naming them. The first is a verb in the third person plural with no subject: *Dicen que va a llover*, *Me robaron la bicicleta*. It means "some people", and you do not know who, or do not want to say. It never includes the speaker. The second is *uno* (or *una*, when a woman speaks), which means "a person" and does include the speaker: *Uno nunca sabe*.

sections.title: Three patterns
rows: They say the director is resigning. (a rumour)
Somebody stole my bicycle. (an unknown doer)
Someone is at the door. (a doer you cannot see)
You learn with time. (a woman speaking)

items.spanish: Dicen que mañana va a llover.
items.english: They say it is going to rain tomorrow.

items.spanish: Aquí no dejan entrar a nadie.
items.english: They do not let anybody in here.

items.spanish: Cuando uno viaja mucho, extraña su casa.
items.english: When you travel a lot, you miss your home.

sections.content: The verb must be plural: *Dicen que…* means "they say", while *Dice que…* means "he or she says". With *uno* the verb is singular and the possessive is *su*, because *uno* is a third-person word: *Uno cuida su salud*. Use *dicen* for rumours and news you pass on, and *uno* for a general truth that also applies to you.
